Baby & Child

Can you grow taller after puberty? What healthy habits can and cannot do

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Healthy habits help children and teenagers develop well. Whether more height is possible depends mainly on remaining growth, not on finding the right stretching routine or supplement. Here is how to separate useful support from unrealistic promises.

Can you grow taller after puberty?

The answer depends on whether growth is still taking place. Puberty is a process lasting several years, not one event. Starting puberty, having a first period or noticing a deeper voice does not necessarily mean that all height growth has finished. Some adolescents continue growing after these changes, while others are already close to adult height.

Once the growth plates in the long bones have fused, food, exercise, stretching and supplements cannot restart ordinary bone lengthening. Healthy habits remain valuable for strength, comfort and long-term health. They should not be sold as a way to add a promised number of centimetres after skeletal maturity.

Growth plates explain the difference

Growth plates are areas of developing cartilage near the ends of long bones. During childhood and adolescence, they allow bones to lengthen. As skeletal maturity is reached, these areas are replaced by mature bone. The timing varies, so one age such as eighteen or twenty cannot tell you everyone’s remaining growth potential.

A clinician may use the growth record, examination and, when appropriate, a hand and wrist X-ray to assess bone age. A person cannot reliably judge whether the plates are open from their shoe size, facial hair or an online photograph. Bone-age estimates help clinical decisions but do not provide a guaranteed final height.

Puberty changes the pace of growth

Growth is faster in infancy, steadier through much of childhood and faster again during the pubertal growth spurt. Girls usually have their peak spurt earlier in puberty than boys. Growth generally slows after the first menstrual period, but the amount remaining varies. A first period is not the same as completion of all puberty.

Statements that everyone gains another two to seven centimetres after puberty, or that every child from age one onward grows at the same yearly rate, are too rigid. A sequence of accurate measurements tells more than a single age-based promise. Delayed puberty can shift growth later, but unexpected delay should still be assessed.

Genes matter, but a percentage is not a personal formula

Height is strongly influenced by many inherited gene variants. Family heights can help a clinician estimate a broad expected range. Nutrition, chronic disease, hormones and the timing of puberty also affect growth, so children from the same family do not necessarily end up the same height.

Estimates describing how much variation in height is associated with genetics do not divide one person into a fixed genetic portion and an adjustable lifestyle portion. They cannot tell a teenager how many extra centimetres a diet or exercise programme will produce. The useful aim is to support normal growth and identify treatable problems.

1. Eat enough and include a variety of foods

A growing body needs sufficient overall energy as well as protein, vitamins and minerals. Include a range of vegetables, fruit, grains and protein foods such as beans, lentils, eggs, fish, meat, nuts or seeds as appropriate for age, allergies and food preferences. A varied pattern is more helpful than looking for a single height-increasing food.

Restrictive dieting can make it harder to meet nutritional needs. Fat is also part of a balanced diet and should not be eliminated in pursuit of height. If appetite is poor, food access is difficult, weight is falling or an exclusion diet is needed, ask for practical nutrition support. These issues deserve care rather than blame.

Calcium and vitamin D support bone health

Calcium is available from milk, yoghurt and other dairy foods, calcium-fortified alternatives, some leafy vegetables and canned fish eaten with their soft bones. Foods differ substantially in the amount and availability of calcium they provide. Check labels on plant-based drinks rather than assuming every alternative has the same nutrients as milk.

Vitamin D helps the body use calcium. Sources include oily fish and appropriately fortified foods; egg yolks provide smaller amounts. Some people need a supplement because of age, diet or a medical risk. These nutrients support healthy bones, but extra amounts do not make mature bones longer. A clinician can help distinguish an inadequate intake from a need for investigation.

2. Protect regular, sufficient sleep

Sleep supports health and development, and growth-hormone release is linked with sleep. That does not mean that sleeping longer than needed will increase adult height. A consistent routine and adequate opportunity to sleep are more useful than a promise to gain centimetres by staying in bed.

CDC guidance lists nine to twelve hours for ages six to twelve, eight to ten hours for ages thirteen to seventeen, and at least seven hours for most adults aged eighteen to sixty. Individual needs and sleep quality also matter. Persistent snoring, breathing pauses or exhaustion despite enough time asleep should be discussed with a clinician.

3. Exercise for fitness, strength and enjoyment

Swimming, cycling, running, skipping, climbing, push-ups and other age-appropriate activities can support fitness, coordination and wellbeing. Running and jumping provide weight-bearing activity for bones, while swimming and cycling offer other useful benefits. There is no special sport that guarantees a taller adult body.

For most children and adolescents aged six to seventeen, the general aim is at least sixty minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity a day, with suitable muscle- and bone-strengthening activities included during the week. Start from the person’s ability and circumstances, and adapt for disability or illness. Enjoyment and consistency matter more than using exercise as a punishment for body size.

Stretching, hanging and strength training have limits

Stretching and yoga can improve flexibility, balance and body awareness. Pull-ups and other strengthening exercises can build muscle when performed safely. Hanging from a bar does not reopen growth plates or permanently lengthen the legs or spine. Stop an exercise that causes pain rather than assuming discomfort means growth is happening.

Appropriately designed, supervised strength training has not been shown to stunt normal growth. Good technique, manageable loads and suitable supervision are important. Unsupervised maximal lifting or training through an injury can be harmful. A coach or physiotherapist should focus on safe movement and gradual progress, without height guarantees.

4. Use supplements for a real need

A supplement may be useful when dietary intake is inadequate or a deficiency has been identified. Treating a deficiency can support a growing child’s health; taking more than needed does not bypass the limits set by skeletal maturity. Calcium and vitamin D are not universal height treatments or a guarantee against future osteoporosis.

High doses can cause harm, and some products marketed for growth contain unclear combinations of ingredients. Ask a clinician or pharmacist about the actual ingredient, reason for taking it and appropriate amount. Avoid stacking several products with overlapping vitamins. A dramatic before-and-after photograph is not reliable evidence that a supplement lengthened bones.

Growth hormone is a specialist treatment

Growth hormone can help some children with a diagnosed deficiency or another recognized indication. Treatment requires an assessment and monitoring; short stature alone does not prove deficiency. Other causes of slow growth, such as thyroid disease, coeliac disease, inadequate nutrition or chronic illness, need their own treatment.

After growth plates have closed, growth hormone does not make an adult taller. Excess hormone can instead enlarge tissues and cause serious health problems. Adults with true hormone deficiency may need specialist replacement for other reasons, which is different from using hormones for height. Do not use injected hormones or products claiming to stimulate them without appropriate medical care.

5. Improve comfort and posture without height promises

A comfortable upright posture can change how tall someone appears and help reduce strain. Adjust the desk or chair to fit the person, take movement breaks and use suitable strengthening or flexibility exercises. Avoid treating posture as a test of discipline: pain, fatigue, disability and the working environment can all affect how someone sits or stands.

A pillow, standing desk or posture brace is not a guaranteed cure, and a brace should not be prescribed simply from a photograph. Persistent pain, an unusual spinal curve or movement difficulty may need a clinical or physiotherapy assessment. Posture work supports function; it does not add length to fused long bones.

New loss of height needs a different assessment

An adult who has become noticeably shorter should not automatically assume that slouching is the only explanation. Changes in the spine, including vertebral fractures associated with osteoporosis, can reduce height. Back pain or a new stooped shape deserves attention, particularly when fracture risk is increased.

Ask a clinician about a reliable measurement and whether bone-health assessment is needed. Do not begin forceful stretching to regain lost height or buy a supplement as a substitute for evaluating new symptoms. Maintaining bone health and treating a fracture are different goals from increasing the final height reached after puberty.

6. Ask for review when the growth pattern is concerning

Arrange a review if a child is growing much more slowly than before, moving downward across growth-chart lines, is far below the family’s expected pattern or has concerning pubertal delay. Poor weight gain, persistent digestive symptoms or other illness also adds context. Many shorter children are healthy, including those with familial short stature or constitutional delay.

Bring previous measurements and information about parental heights, puberty timing, medicines and health conditions. Depending on the findings, the clinician may recommend observation, selected blood tests, a bone-age assessment or referral to paediatric endocrinology. Not every short child needs every test, but repeatedly dismissing a changing growth pattern can delay useful care.

Keep the goal focused on health and confidence

Choose a few realistic habits: regular meals, enough sleep, enjoyable activity and follow-up of any identified concern. Measure growth at sensible intervals with a consistent method rather than repeatedly checking throughout the day. Different measuring techniques can create apparent changes that are not true growth.

Height is not a measure of worth, attractiveness or future success. Avoid teasing, comparisons or promises that a child could be taller if they tried harder. If anxiety about height is affecting eating, exercise, friendships or mood, bring that into the health conversation too. Support can address distress even when no treatment to increase height is appropriate.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Interpret height using repeated measurements, puberty stage, family context and clinical assessment rather than a universal age cutoff.

Nutrition, activity and sleep support health; none reopens fused growth plates. Hormone treatment requires a recognized medical indication.

How BeMama can help

Help a young person feel supported in their body while checking any genuine change in growth.

When to seek help

Seek assessment for slowing growth, concerning pubertal delay, persistent symptoms or new adult height loss. Avoid unprescribed hormones and high-dose height supplements.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Puberty is a process; some growth may remain after its first visible changes.
  • Once growth plates fuse, ordinary diet and exercise cannot lengthen the long bones.
  • The six useful approaches are adequate nutrition, sleep, activity, targeted supplements, comfortable posture and appropriate clinical review.
  • A healthy shorter child does not automatically need treatment; a changing growth pattern deserves attention.

Frequently asked questions

Can I add two to seven centimetres after puberty?

There is no universal amount. If puberty is still progressing and growth plates remain open, some growth may remain. After fusion, ordinary lifestyle measures do not lengthen the long bones.

Does a first period mean all growth has stopped?

No. Height growth usually slows after menarche, but the amount remaining varies. Pubertal stage and the growth record provide more context than that event alone.

Do all growth plates close at eighteen?

No. Skeletal maturity varies. A clinician may use the examination and, when indicated, a bone-age X-ray to assess remaining growth.

Will swimming, skipping or hanging make me taller?

These activities can support fitness or strength, but they do not reopen growth plates or guarantee extra adult height.

Does strength training stunt a child’s growth?

Appropriately designed and supervised training is not shown to stunt normal growth. Technique, manageable loads and injury prevention matter.

Will more calcium or vitamin D increase height?

Correcting an inadequate intake or deficiency supports health, but extra supplements do not lengthen mature bones. High doses can be harmful.

Can extra sleep create another growth spurt?

Adequate sleep supports development and wellbeing. Sleeping beyond your needs has not been shown to restart growth after skeletal maturity.

Can growth hormone make an adult taller?

Not after growth plates have fused. Growth hormone has specific medical uses, but excess hormone can cause harm and is not a general adult height treatment.

When should a shorter child see a clinician?

Arrange review for slowed growth, downward crossing of chart lines, an unexpected family-height pattern, concerning pubertal delay or symptoms of illness. Short stature alone is not a diagnosis.

What if an adult has lost height?

Discuss it with a clinician, especially with back pain or a new stooped posture. Spinal changes or fractures may need assessment; do not assume posture exercises will solve the cause.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
